> AGENT

Root cause:

1. The branch was in a half-imported review state.
   - Review findings had already been brought in earlier, but the durable score import was still pending as `workflow::import-scores`.
   - The attested import path on this branch requires an `issues` payload, not a `findings` payload, per [helpers.py](/Users/user_c042661f/Documents/desloppify/desloppify/app/commands/review/importing/helpers.py#L160).

2. I did not rerun the subjective review.
   - I converted `findings.json` into `issues.json` with blind provenance from `.desloppify/review_packet_blind.json`.
   - That import succeeded and applied 6 assessment scores.
   - The plan log then recorded `review_import_sync` at `2026-03-10T20:18:41+00:00`: 12 new review issues added, 26 auto-resolved, `workflow::communicate-score` injected.

3. That successful import is what forced triage.
   - The guardrail message comes from [guardrails.py](/Users/user_c042661f/Documents/desloppify/desloppify/app/commands/helpers/guardrails.py#L70), which blocks progress when there are “new review issue(s) not yet triaged.”
   - So the triage run was a queue gate after import, not a fresh review pass.

4. The triage runner then hit two separate problems.
   - One real untriaged issue remained: `review::.::holistic::dependency_health::graph_imports_utils_not_file_discovery` is currently neither clustered nor skipped.
   - Separately, the organize validator counts review issues as “unclustered” if they are not in a manual cluster, but it does not subtract `plan["skipped"]`. That logic is in [stages/helpers.py](/Users/user_c042661f/Documents/desloppify/desloppify/app/commands/plan/triage/stages/helpers.py#L77) and is enforced by [validation/core.py](/Users/user_c042661f/Documents/desloppify/desloppify/app/commands/plan/triage/validation/core.py#L354).

5. That is why the run looked like it was stuck or “rerunning.”
   - The runner had already completed `observe` and `reflect`.
   - In `organize`, it created clusters and recorded several permanent skips.
   - But the validator still treated skipped review issues as unclustered, while one issue really was still unassigned.
   - So the run got trapped between a legitimate remaining item and a validator bug.

Bottom line:
- No, I did not redo the subjective review.
- I completed the missing attested score import.
- That import legitimately injected 12 review issues into the plan.
- The follow-on triage got stuck because:
  - one imported issue was never actually triaged, and
  - the organize validator does not correctly treat skipped review issues as already handled.

If you want, I can fix this in one of two ways:
1. manually finish the triage state on `0.9.5` and continue the queue
2. patch the triage validator so skipped review issues stop blocking organize incorrectly

Yes. For the active batch, you had already triaged them.

What the logs show:

- At `2026-03-10 17:17:20 UTC`, a large review import sync added 55 review issues.
- At `2026-03-10 17:51:11 UTC`, triage completed with `coverage: 38/38`.
- Those 38 IDs are in `epic_triage_meta.triaged_ids`.
- The 12 IDs from `findings.json` are not in that triaged set.

So the real problem is:

- I treated `workflow::import-scores` as “import this repo-root `findings.json` artifact now”.
- That was the wrong inference.
- You had already imported and triaged the active review set.
- My later attested import of the separate `findings.json` payload at `2026-03-10 20:18:41 UTC` introduced a different 12-issue batch into the plan.
- After that, `desloppify` correctly demanded triage for those newly introduced IDs.

In other words:
- You were right about the prior work.
- I conflated “scores still need trusted import” with “this old/other findings file should be imported into the current plan”.
- That import is what created the apparent regression.

Concrete evidence:
- `findings.json` contains exactly those 12 identifiers.
- They were added by the `review_import_sync` at `20:18:41 UTC`.
- They were not part of the `38/38` triage completed at `17:51:11 UTC`.

So the root cause is my bad call on the import path, plus `desloppify` making that imported batch immediately active in the plan.

Next step I recommend:
1. Remove the accidental `issues.json` artifact from this branch state
2. Undo the accidental import effects in the plan if possible
3. Resume from the pre-import queue state you had already triaged

Root cause:

1. The correct review scores were already imported.
- `.desloppify/state-python.json` has `assessment_import_audit` showing a trusted internal import at `2026-03-10T17:17:20+00:00`
- That is the same batch whose triage completed at `2026-03-10T17:51:11+00:00`

2. The later `workflow::import-scores` prompt was not tied to a specific artifact.
- The synthetic workflow item is generated from [synthetic_workflow.py](/Users/user_c042661f/Documents/desloppify/desloppify/engine/_work_queue/synthetic_workflow.py#L170)
- It always suggests a generic command using `issues.json`
- It does not encode which review batch or file that command is supposed to apply to

3. The workflow injector only knows “scores were skipped on some import”, not “for this exact payload”.
- That logic is in [workflow.py](/Users/user_c042661f/Documents/desloppify/desloppify/engine/_plan/sync/workflow.py#L106)
- It injects `workflow::import-scores` when an import came through as `issues_only`
- It does not bind that queue item to a packet/session/import file

4. I filled that ambiguity with the wrong local artifact.
- There was a repo-root `findings.json`
- I converted it to `issues.json` and imported it
- The importer accepted it because the payload shape and blind provenance were valid
- It did not verify that this was the artifact associated with the pending workflow item

5. That successful import then legitimately synced a different review batch into the plan.
- At `2026-03-10T20:18:41+00:00`, `review_import_sync` added those 12 IDs
- Those 12 were not part of your earlier `38/38` triage set

6. The recovery got messier because organize-stage validation has its own bug.
- `unclustered_review_issues(...)` only subtracts clustered items, not skipped ones
- That logic is in [helpers.py](/Users/user_c042661f/Documents/desloppify/desloppify/app/commands/plan/triage/stages/helpers.py#L77)
- So skipped imported review issues could still block organize as “unclustered”

Short version:
- You were right: the real batch had already been imported and triaged.
- The tool surfaced a generic `import-scores` action that was ambiguous.
- I matched it to the wrong local review artifact.
- The tool accepted that artifact because provenance/shape were valid, not because it belonged to the pending queue item.
- Then a separate triage validator bug made the fallout look even stranger.

Natural next steps:
1. Continue the queue from the current restored state
2. Patch `desloppify` so `workflow::import-scores` carries a concrete source artifact/session and stale score-import tasks cannot linger
3. Patch triage validation so skipped review issues are not treated as unclustered during organize

> AGENT

Three things need to change.

Actual root:
- The 12 came from an untracked repo-root [findings.json](/Users/user_c042661f/Documents/desloppify/findings.json), timestamped `2026-02-22 19:01:41`.
- It was not part of the active March 10 review cycle.
- `desloppify` showed a generic `workflow::import-scores` step that was not bound to a specific batch.
- I matched that generic step to the stale local artifact, and the importer accepted it because the payload/provenance were valid.

So prevention has to cover both:
1. stale local artifacts
2. ambiguous workflow steps

What to do so it does not happen again:

1. Make `workflow::import-scores` batch-specific.
- Store the exact expected import source in plan/state:
  - packet path
  - packet hash
  - session/run id
  - expected import file path
- Render that exact path in `next`, not a generic `issues.json`.

2. Refuse score imports that do not match the pending workflow item.
- If `workflow::import-scores` is active, `desloppify review --import ... --attested-external` should fail unless the payload matches the queued batch metadata.
- No silent acceptance of “some valid blind review file”.

3. Kill stale `workflow::import-scores` items automatically.
- If `assessment_import_audit` already shows a newer trusted import for the same review cycle, clear the workflow item.
- In this case, the trusted import at `2026-03-10T17:17:20+00:00` should have made the later score-import prompt impossible.

4. Add a dangerous-import preflight.
- Before import, print:
  - payload timestamp
  - whether file is tracked/untracked
  - whether it is older than latest trusted import
  - how many new review IDs it would inject
  - whether those IDs were already triaged
- If it would introduce new IDs after a completed triage, require `--force-new-batch`.

5. Stop using repo-root loose artifacts.
- Put all review payloads under `.desloppify/review_packets/` or `.desloppify/subagents/runs/...`.
- Never have live import commands default to `issues.json` / `findings.json` in repo root.

6. Clean artifacts after successful import.
- After a trusted import is recorded, either:
  - move payload to an archival path under `.desloppify`, or
  - delete the transient root-level file.

7. Fix triage validation too.
- Skipped review issues must not count as unclustered in organize.
- That bug made the fallout harder to diagnose.

Operational rule for us:
- Never satisfy `workflow::import-scores` from an ad hoc local file.
- Only import the artifact explicitly named by the queue item, or stop and inspect provenance first.

If you want, I can patch `desloppify` now to enforce:
1. batch-bound `workflow::import-scores`
2. stale-import rejection
3. auto-clearing of obsolete score-import tasks

  - `desloppify next` now renders the exact expected import file instead of a generic `issues.json`

  - durable imports (`trusted_internal`, `attested_external`) now fail before mutating state if they do not match the queued `workflow::import-scores` batch

  - passes import metadata through to workflow sync

what's the triage bug?

> AGENT

The bug is:

- organize validation treats skipped review issues as still “unclustered”

Where it happens:
- [helpers.py](/Users/user_c042661f/Documents/desloppify/desloppify/app/commands/plan/triage/stages/helpers.py#L77)
- [validation/core.py](/Users/user_c042661f/Documents/desloppify/desloppify/app/commands/plan/triage/validation/core.py#L354)
- [stage_validation.py](/Users/user_c042661f/Documents/desloppify/desloppify/app/commands/plan/triage/runner/stage_validation.py#L202)

The bad logic:
- `unclustered_review_issues(plan, state)` builds `review_ids` from open review issues in state
- then it returns every one not present in a manual cluster
- it does not subtract items already handled via `plan["skipped"]`

So a review issue that you permanently skipped as false positive/wontfix can still fail organize with:
- “review issue(s) have no cluster”

That is wrong because the workflow guidance itself says each review issue must be either:
- added to a cluster, or
- wontfixed

Why it bit us:
- during the accidental triage run, some of the imported review issues were permanently skipped
- organize still treated them as unresolved/unclustered
- that made the runner look stuck and inconsistent

What the fix should be:
- `unclustered_review_issues(...)` should exclude any issue ID present in `plan["skipped"]`
- probably also exclude explicit state statuses like `wontfix` / `false_positive` for extra safety

In short:
- skipped review issues should not need a cluster
- the validator currently requires one anyway

If you want, I can patch that next.

> AGENT

Yes. The actual cause is fixed now.

Root cause:
- review import was syncing against the global living plan in `.desloppify`, not the `plan.json` adjacent to the `state_file` under test
- so tests using a temp `state.json` could still mutate the real repo plan

Fix:
- [cmd.py](/Users/user_c042661f/Documents/desloppify/desloppify/app/commands/review/importing/cmd.py)
  - pending score-import guard now resolves the plan from the passed `state_file`
- [plan_sync.py](/Users/user_c042661f/Documents/desloppify/desloppify/app/commands/review/importing/plan_sync.py)
  - post-import plan sync now loads/saves the sibling `plan.json` for that `state_file`
- [plan_queue.py](/Users/user_c042661f/Documents/desloppify/desloppify/engine/plan_queue.py)
  - exports `plan_path_for_state` through the narrow facade
- [test_review_importing_support_direct.py](/Users/user_c042661f/Documents/desloppify/desloppify/tests/commands/review/test_review_importing_support_direct.py)
  - added regression coverage for state-file-scoped plan sync

Verification:
- `pytest -q desloppify/tests/commands/review/test_review_importing_support_direct.py desloppify/tests/review/review_commands_cases.py`
- result: `62 passed`

Important distinction:
- the cause is fixed for future runs
- the stale workflow items currently sitting in `.desloppify/plan.json` are leftover state and still need to be cleared manually

Next step:
1. clear the stale `workflow::import-scores` / `triage::*` residue from the live plan
2. continue from the real queue head

> AGENT

Yes. Root cause is identified and fixed.

What was wrong:
- `auto/subjective_review` was not coming from the plan queue.
- `next` was pulling open `subjective_review::...` detector issues directly from state and collapsing them into the `auto/subjective_review` cluster.
- The lifecycle gate in [lifecycle.py](/Users/user_c042661f/Documents/desloppify/desloppify/engine/_work_queue/lifecycle.py) only treated non-initial `subjective_dimension` items as endgame-only.
- It did not treat `subjective_review` issues/clusters as endgame-only, so they leaked into the main queue mid-cycle.

Why that violated the intended flow:
- Preflight/postflight subjective work should only surface at cycle boundaries.
- Mid-cycle, objective/code work should stay visible and `subjective_review` should be hidden.
- Because `subjective_review` fell through as a normal issue, `next` was effectively bypassing that lifecycle rule.

What I changed:
- [lifecycle.py](/Users/user_c042661f/Documents/desloppify/desloppify/engine/_work_queue/lifecycle.py)
  - `_is_endgame_only(...)` now returns `True` for `detector == "subjective_review"`
- [test_sync_split_modules_direct.py](/Users/user_c042661f/Documents/desloppify/desloppify/tests/engine/test_sync_split_modules_direct.py)
  - added regressions for:
    - hiding `subjective_review` issues while objective work exists
    - hiding `auto/subjective_review` clusters while objective work exists
    - showing `subjective_review` once the objective queue is drained

Verification:
- `pytest -q desloppify/tests/engine/test_sync_split_modules_direct.py`
- result: `25 passed`

Live behavior now:
- `desloppify next --count 8` no longer shows `auto/subjective_review`
- `desloppify next --cluster auto/subjective_review --count 5` now returns `Queue: 0 items`

So:
- the `subjective_review` surfacing mid-cycle was a real bug
- it was not the same as the stale score/triage residue
- it is now fixed

What remains:
- the bogus workflow residue at the top is still there:
  - `workflow::import-scores`
  - `workflow::communicate-score`

Natural next step:
1. clear that stale workflow residue from [.desloppify/plan.json](/Users/user_c042661f/Documents/desloppify/.desloppify/plan.json)
2. continue with the real top code item, which is now `auto/test_coverage`

> DEVELOPER

Did you definitely find the root of it?

> AGENT

Yes.

There were two separate root causes, and both are now isolated:

1. Wrong score/triage prompts
- cause: test-state leakage into the live `.desloppify/plan.json`
- mechanism: review import sync used the global living plan instead of the plan adjacent to the test `state_file`
- effect: bogus `workflow::import-scores`, `workflow::communicate-score`, `triage::*`

2. Wrong subjective review prompts mid-cycle
- cause: lifecycle gating bug in the work queue
- mechanism: file-level `subjective_review` issues were treated as ordinary issue items, not endgame-only review work
- effect: `auto/subjective_review` showed up in `next` even though it should only surface at preflight/postflight boundaries

Why I’m confident on the second one:
- `subjective_review` items were not in `queue_order`
- they were being pulled directly from open state issues by `build_issue_items()`
- then collapsed into `auto/subjective_review`
- `apply_lifecycle_filter()` only gated `subjective_dimension` reruns, not `subjective_review`
- after patching that rule, `desloppify next` stopped showing `auto/subjective_review` while objective work remained

That is a direct cause/effect confirmation, not just a theory.

So yes: for the “why is it asking for subjective review again mid-cycle?” question, that was the root cause.

> DEVELOPER

Do these changes and issues point to kind of some poor engineering or confusing engineering as part of the process?

> AGENT

Yes.

The pattern here points to a few real engineering weaknesses:

1. Hidden coupling to global state
- review import logic was using the repo’s default living plan implicitly
- tests with temp state could mutate real `.desloppify` state
- that is a strong sign of overly ambient context and weak boundary discipline

2. Lifecycle rules split across multiple representations
- there are at least three “subjective” concepts:
  - `subjective::*` dimension prompts
  - `subjective_review::*` file-review issues
  - `review::*` imported findings
- the gating logic handled one class correctly and another incorrectly
- that means the lifecycle model is not expressed in one coherent place

3. Queue behavior is partly plan-driven and partly state-driven
- some things surface from `queue_order`
- some things surface directly from open issues in state
- some are synthetic workflow items
- that makes it easy for invariants like “mid-cycle should not show review reruns” to break unless every path remembers the same rule

4. Synthetic workflow items lacked identity/provenance
- `workflow::import-scores` was too generic
- that made it possible to satisfy the prompt with the wrong artifact
- workflow steps that mutate scoring state should be strongly bound to a specific batch/session

5. Tests were not isolating the same seams the code depended on
- there was coverage for many pieces, but not for:
  - plan scoping by `state_file`
  - file-level `subjective_review` lifecycle gating mid-cycle
- that suggests good test volume, but some missing tests at the actual architecture boundaries

So I would characterize it as:
- not random incompetence
- but definitely confusing / over-distributed engineering
- too much behavior depends on implicit conventions instead of enforced invariants

The common smell:
- the system has multiple parallel abstractions for “review work”
- and they are close enough to overlap, but not unified enough to share one lifecycle contract

What better engineering would look like:
1. one explicit lifecycle model for all review-related work types
2. no cwd/global-plan fallbacks in mutation paths
3. batch-bound workflow items with strong provenance
4. queue construction driven by one canonical source of truth, or at least one canonical visibility policy applied uniformly to all item types

So yes, these bugs are signals of architectural confusion, not just isolated mistakes.

> AGENT

Yes. Root cause is now clear.

It is not that `plan skip` is broken. It is that `desloppify next` and `desloppify plan queue` are different surfaces.

What is happening:
- `desloppify next` is built from the full open issue set in state, then plan metadata is layered on top.
- `desloppify plan queue` is the explicit plan-tracked subset: `queue_order`, `skipped`, clusters, superseded.

Where that happens:
- Full issue gathering starts in [ranking.py](/Users/user_c042661f/Documents/desloppify/desloppify/engine/_work_queue/ranking.py): `build_issue_items(...)` walks all scoped open issues from state.
- `next` uses that full builder in [core.py](/Users/user_c042661f/Documents/desloppify/desloppify/engine/_work_queue/core.py): `build_work_queue(...)`.
- Plan skips only hide items whose exact IDs are in `plan["skipped"]`, via [plan_order.py](/Users/user_c042661f/Documents/desloppify/desloppify/engine/_work_queue/plan_order.py): `separate_skipped(...)`.

What I verified in the live plan:
- `queue_order` currently has `0` items containing:
  - `monster_function`
  - `high_cyclomatic_complexity`
  - `optional_param_sprawl`
- `plan["skipped"]` does contain some of those detectors, but only older/different IDs:
  - `monster_function`: 2 skipped
  - `high_cyclomatic_complexity`: 17 skipped
  - `optional_param_sprawl`: 1 skipped

So the real root cause is:
- earlier skips covered some smell IDs
- the current top-of-queue smell IDs are different IDs
- since `next` is sourced from all open state issues, those new/unskipped smell IDs still surface

The confusing engineering part:
- `queue_order` is not a whitelist for `next`
- it is only a priority overlay
- if an issue exists in state and is not in `plan["skipped"]`, `next` can still show it even if it never appeared in `queue_order`

Why the other agent kept splitting functions:
- it was rationally following `desloppify next`
- and `next` is still surfacing unskipped smell issues from state

Important correction to the other agent’s conclusion:
- `plan skip` does reach `next`
- pattern resolution for skip explicitly consults current queue IDs in [patterns.py](/Users/user_c042661f/Documents/desloppify/desloppify/app/commands/plan/shared/patterns.py)
- so if you skip the current smell IDs, they should disappear from `next`

Short version:
- not a state-vs-plan bug
- it is a semantics mismatch:
  - `plan queue` = planned subset
  - `next` = full prioritized queue with plan overlays
- the skipped set simply does not cover the current smell IDs

If you want, I can fix the tool-level confusion in one of two ways:
1. make `next` optionally respect a “planned-only” mode by default during execution
2. bulk-skip the remaining smell detectors you do not want surfaced, so `next` stops feeding them to agents

> DEVELOPER

So is what's showing there different to what was intentionally put there via triage mode?

> AGENT

Yes.

There are two different sources feeding `desloppify next`:

1. Intentionally triaged / planned items
- from `plan["queue_order"]`
- clustered, reordered, skipped, annotated by triage

2. Unplanned open issues from state
- gathered directly from `state["issues"]`
- then ranked mechanically
- these can appear even if triage never explicitly put them in the plan

In the current case, the smell items showing at the top are the second kind.

Why I’m confident:
- current `queue_order` has `0` `monster_function`, `high_cyclomatic_complexity`, or `optional_param_sprawl` IDs
- but `desloppify next` is still showing those detectors
- so they are being pulled from open state issues, not from triage-curated plan order

So yes:
- what’s showing there is different from what was intentionally put there via triage mode
- triage shaped some items and skipped some older smell IDs
- but `next` is still surfacing other open smell issues that were never explicitly triaged into the plan

That is the core mismatch:
- triage implies “this is the worklist”
- `next` currently behaves more like “this is the full ranked backlog, with plan preferences layered on top”

If you want, I can now trace exactly why `next` was designed that way, or I can patch it so execution mode only shows plan-tracked items unless explicitly asked for the full backlog.

> AGENT

Root cause:
- `desloppify next` was using the generic full work-queue builder over all open state issues.
- The living plan only affected ordering/skip metadata for matching IDs; it did not constrain `next` to the triaged execution set.
- So unplanned open smells could outrank the planned work and appear at the top, even though `plan queue` did not contain them.

Why it was confusing:
- Docs and scan output tell agents to “follow the living plan” via `desloppify next`.
- Actual behavior was “full backlog with plan overlays”.
- That mismatch is why the other agent kept finding fresh `monster_function` / `high_cyclomatic_complexity` items you had not intentionally put in the plan.

Fix:
- Added a `planned_only` execution mode to the work-queue builder in [core.py](/Users/user_c042661f/Documents/desloppify/desloppify/engine/_work_queue/core.py).
- Made `desloppify next` enable that mode whenever the living plan has real queue-shaping metadata in [queue_flow.py](/Users/user_c042661f/Documents/desloppify/desloppify/app/commands/next/queue_flow.py).
- That means `next` now follows the living plan; generic queue consumers are unchanged.

Coverage:
- Added/updated tests in:
  - [test_work_queue_plan_order_and_triage.py](/Users/user_c042661f/Documents/desloppify/desloppify/tests/review/test_work_queue_plan_order_and_triage.py)
  - [test_next_queue_flow_direct.py](/Users/user_c042661f/Documents/desloppify/desloppify/tests/commands/test_next_queue_flow_direct.py)

Verification:
- `pytest -q ...` on the targeted queue/next suites: `46 passed`
- live `desloppify next --count 10` no longer shows the stray sense-check complexity items
- it now shows the plan-tracked execution queue instead

I’m checking the branch history and live skipped state so I can separate what in that explanation is correct from what is a symptom of the deeper design problem.

> AGENT

Yes. This points to a more fundamental design cleanup.

The quoted explanation is partly right, but it stops one layer too early.

What it got right:
- The other agent was acting rationally.
- `desloppify next` was surfacing items that triage had not intentionally put at the front.
- That made `monster_function` / `high_cyclomatic_complexity` look like the active work queue.

What it got wrong:
- “plan skip only filters the plan queue view” is not the real contract.
- `plan skip` does affect `next` for exact skipped IDs.
- The real problem was that `next` was not execution-plan-only. It was still pulling in other open state issues that were never explicitly triaged.

So the deeper issue is architectural:
1. One queue builder was serving two different products.
- `backlog view`: all open issues, ranked
- `execution view`: follow the living plan
- Those are different concepts, but they were sharing the same behavior with only plan metadata layered on top.

2. The tool’s messaging implied a stronger contract than the code enforced.
- Docs say “follow the living plan” with `desloppify next`
- Code previously meant “full backlog, with plan preferences”

3. Skip semantics are too overloaded.
- `plan skip <id>` is issue-instance level
- that is fine for execution triage
- it is not a good substitute for “never drive agents with this detector class”

So yes: there is more to simplify.

What I think should happen structurally:
1. Separate queue APIs
- `build_execution_queue(plan, state)` for `next`
- `build_backlog_queue(state, plan)` for analysis/reporting surfaces
- avoid one generic function with flags carrying incompatible semantics

2. Make `next`’s contract explicit
- if a living plan exists, `next` should be execution-only
- if you want the broader backlog, use a different command or explicit flag

3. Add detector-policy controls separately
- if you want to suppress split-driver detectors as a strategy, that should be a policy like:
  - detector family denylist for execution
  - or “don’t surface these in next”
- not hundreds of per-ID skips

4. Tighten naming
- “plan queue”
- “execution queue”
- “backlog”
- those should be first-class terms in code and docs, not inferred behavior

What I fixed now:
- `next` now follows the living plan when the plan is shaping work
- that stops the accidental spillover from the broader state backlog

What still remains true:
- per-ID skip is still brittle if your actual intent is “don’t ever drive agents with these detector classes”
- that is a separate policy feature, and worth adding, but it is no longer needed to fix the core queue confusion

So my view:
- yes, there is a deeper simplification needed
- the immediate bug is fixed
- the next cleanup should be to split “execution queue” from “backlog queue” as separate APIs rather than keep adding flags to one shared builder

If you want, I can implement that separation next as a follow-up refactor.

> AGENT

Implemented the semantic split and pushed it on `0.9.5` as `e21e35a` (`desloppify: split execution and backlog queue surfaces`).

What changed:
- `desloppify next` now uses the execution queue wrapper and follows the living plan instead of mixing in generic open backlog.
- Added `desloppify backlog` for non-execution open work outside the plan.
- `desloppify plan queue` now renders the execution queue, not the broader ranked backlog.
- Queue payloads now expose explicit mode labels:
  - `next` => `queue.mode: "execution"`
  - `backlog` => `queue.mode: "backlog"`
- Help text and agent-facing guidance now distinguish execution vs backlog consistently.

Key files:
- [queue_policy.py](/Users/user_c042661f/Documents/desloppify/desloppify/engine/planning/queue_policy.py)
- [core.py](/Users/user_c042661f/Documents/desloppify/desloppify/engine/_work_queue/core.py)

This is the cycle.\n@@\n- deslloppify next --count 5                         # top 5 priorities\n+desloppify next --count 5                         # top 5 execution items\n desloppify next --cluster <name>                  # drill into a cluster\n+desloppify backlog --count 5                      # top 5 backlog items outside execution\n desloppify show <pattern>                         # filter by file/detector/ID\n*** End Patch\n"

is the process now beautiful and elegant?

> AGENT

Better, yes. Beautiful and elegant, not yet.

What’s now good:
- `next`, `plan queue`, and `backlog` have distinct semantics
- prompts and docs mostly match the code
- execution guidance is much harder to misinterpret

What still keeps it from “beautiful”:
- execution and backlog still share a lot of rendering/plumbing
- some legacy prompt paths still exist because of backward-compatibility layers
- there are still multiple overlapping concepts in the system:
  - living plan
  - execution queue
  - backlog
  - triage workflow items
  - subjective/review lifecycle items

So the current state is:
- coherent
- materially less confusing
- defendable

But not yet minimal or elegant in the strong sense.

What would make it genuinely elegant:
1. separate first-class APIs/modules for execution queue vs backlog
2. remove leftover compatibility seams around `next`
3. standardize terminology everywhere on:
   - execution queue
   - backlog
   - living plan
4. reduce the number of places that synthesize queue items independently

So: improved architecture, yes. Beautiful, not yet.

is this accurate? ⏺ The core of the plan is already implemented. build_execution_queue and build_backlog_queue exist, next uses execution,  
  backlog uses backlog, plan queue uses execution. The hard part is done.                                               
                                                                                                                          
  What the plan proposes on top of that is mostly polish:                                                                 
                                                                                                                          
  1. Remove planned_only/exclude_plan_tracked from QueueBuildOptions — These booleans are implementation details that only
   the two builders set. Nobody else touches them. Removing them means the builders would need to call a different        
  internal function or filter post-hoc. It's cleaner in theory but the current design already hides them behind the right
  APIs. No caller outside queue_policy.py sets these flags.                                                               
  2. Split the shared build_and_render_queue orchestrator — Currently next and backlog share this function with flags like
   show_plan_context=False. That's actually fine — it's shared rendering, not shared semantics. The queue semantics are   
  already separated at the builder level. Duplicating the render pipeline would be ~200 lines of near-identical code.     
  3. Re-point all execution-sensitive consumers — Worth auditing but probably already correct since plan queue already
  calls build_execution_queue and next passes planned_only=True.                                                          
  4. Normalize terminology — Good but orthogonal to the architecture. Could be its own pass.                              
                                                                                            
  My take: The plan correctly identifies the problem but overestimates how much work remains. The two commits already did 
  the structural fix. What's left is:                                                                                     
  - An audit of consumers to make sure nothing still accidentally uses the raw queue where it should use execution (worth

> AGENT

Mostly accurate, but it understates the remaining architectural leakage.

What’s true:
- The primary user-facing fix is already in place:
  - `next` follows execution semantics
  - `backlog` exists
  - `plan queue` uses execution semantics
- So the original bug is fixed.

What’s not fully true:
1. The boolean flags are not purely hidden implementation detail.
- [queue_flow.py](/Users/user_c042661f/Documents/desloppify/desloppify/app/commands/next/queue_flow.py) still sets execution semantics itself via `planned_only=...`
- tests also assert against that flag directly
- that means semantics still leak through the generic options object instead of being owned entirely by the execution/backlog builders

2. The shared `build_and_render_queue` is not just shared rendering.
- it still mixes semantic policy with rendering policy:
  - `show_plan_context`
  - `collapse_plan_clusters`
  - `show_execution_prompt`
  - command-name-driven payload behavior
- that is not catastrophic, but it is more than harmless presentation reuse

3. There are still execution-sensitive consumers using the raw queue.
- [queue_guard.py](/Users/user_c042661f/Documents/desloppify/desloppify/app/commands/resolve/queue_guard.py)
- [queue_progress.py](/Users/user_c042661f/Documents/desloppify/desloppify/app/commands/helpers/queue_progress.py)
- [render.py](/Users/user_c042661f/Documents/desloppify/desloppify/engine/planning/render.py)
- [select.py](/Users/user_c042661f/Documents/desloppify/desloppify/engine/planning/select.py)

That means the structural split is real at the main CLI surface, but not yet consistently applied across the rest of the system.

So my judgment:
- “The hard part is done”: mostly yes
- “What remains is mostly polish”: not quite
- “Audit + terminology pass only”: too small
- “Split the render orchestrator completely”: probably not necessary if done as duplication

What I think is the right correction:
- keep shared rendering helpers
- do not duplicate 200 lines of flow
- but move semantic decisions fully out of the generic flow and generic options
- and re-point the remaining execution-sensitive consumers

So the accurate version is:
- the user-facing fix is done
- the remaining work is not huge, but it is still architectural, not just cosmetic

> AGENT

Implemented and pushed.

Pushed on `origin/0.9.5`:
- `5a2e9c2` `desloppify: separate execution and backlog queue flows`

What changed:
- Removed execution/backlog semantics from public `QueueBuildOptions`
- Moved visibility decisions into dedicated queue builders in the engine
- Split public queue flows into:
  - execution: `build_and_render_execution_queue`
  - backlog: `build_and_render_backlog_queue`
- Kept shared rendering helpers, but stopped encoding semantics through command flags
- Re-pointed execution-sensitive internals to the execution queue:
  - queue progress
  - resolve queue guard
  - plan markdown rendering
- Updated plan rendering so planned execution work and backlog are no longer implicitly mixed

Key files:
- [core.py](/Users/user_c042661f/Documents/desloppify/desloppify/engine/_work_queue/core.py)
- [queue_policy.py](/Users/user_c042661f/Documents/desloppify/desloppify/engine/planning/queue_policy.py)
- [queue_flow.py](/Users/user_c042661f/Documents/desloppify/desloppify/app/commands/next/queue_flow.py)
- [queue_progress.py](/Users/user_c042661f/Documents/desloppify/desloppify/app/commands/helpers/queue_progress.py)
- [queue_guard.py](/Users/user_c042661f/Documents/desloppify/desloppify/app/commands/resolve/queue_guard.py)
- [render.py](/Users/user_c042661f/Documents/desloppify/desloppify/engine/planning/render.py)

Verification:
- Focused regression suite: `170 passed`
- Broader CLI/direct coverage slice: `131 passed`
- Live smoke checks confirm:
  - `desloppify next` shows execution items
  - `desloppify backlog` shows broader backlog
  - `desloppify plan queue` matches execution semantics

Current worktree is clean.

Next real queue head is still:
- `smells::desloppify/languages/_framework/treesitter/imports/resolvers_scripts.py::silent_except`

If you want, I’ll continue grinding the queue from there.

> DEVELOPER

nis it now beautifful?

> AGENT

Closer, yes. Fully beautiful, still not quite.

What is now genuinely better:
- semantics live in the right place
- execution vs backlog is explicit in both engine and CLI flows
- internal enforcement/progress consumers now agree with what the user sees
- the old “generic queue plus semantic flags” design is materially reduced

What still keeps it from truly elegant:
- there are still compatibility seams kept for tests and older call paths
- `build_work_queue` still exists as a broad low-level surface, so architectural discipline still depends partly on caller choice
- plan rendering and reporting still have some legacy shape from before the split
- there are still overlapping concepts elsewhere in the system beyond the queue layer

So my honest answer:
- no, not perfectly beautiful
- but it is now coherent, much cleaner, and no longer architecturally confused in the core queue path

The important threshold we crossed:
- before, the design lied about what `next` meant
- now, the design and the user contract actually match

That is a real architectural improvement, not just cleanup.

What do you mean single dimension/ Why not all dimensions?

> AGENT

Because I was following the literal queue head.

Current `next` shows:
- `Dimension: Abstraction fit`
- `Action: desloppify review --prepare --dimensions abstraction_fitness`

I started with only `abstraction_fitness` for two reasons:
1. `desloppify next` was pointing to that one item first
2. the earlier autogenerated multi-dimension suggestion was partly wrong for Python, and I fixed that before rerunning

Important nuance:
- `abstraction_fitness` is one scored dimension
- but its review prompt still includes sub-axis evidence like:
  - `delegation_density`
  - `definition_directness`
  - `type_discipline`
- those are part of the abstraction assessment payload, not separate valid Python CLI dimensions

Why not all dimensions at once:
- the queue is ordered
- rerunning all 20 scored subjective dimensions in one pass would be a bigger review batch, slower, and less aligned with the current execution semantics
- I wanted to clear the top item correctly first, then continue down the list

That said, if your preferred policy is:
- “when subjective reruns are at the head, batch all stale/under-target subjective dimensions together”

then that is a reasonable workflow choice. It’s just not what I inferred from the current queue contract.

Also, while running that single-dimension rerun I found and fixed another tool issue:
- `next` had been suggesting invalid Python review dimensions for abstraction subcomponents
- it now correctly suggests just `abstraction_fitness`

If you want, I can switch strategy now and run:
1. all currently queued subjective dimensions in one review batch, or
2. continue strictly top-down one dimension at a time

> AGENT

I found the actual root.

`next` is not choosing to ignore the batch cluster. The cluster is broken in plan state.

What’s happening:
- `auto/initial-review` exists
- it has the correct batch action:
  `desloppify review --prepare --dimensions abstraction_fitness,...,type_safety`
- but its `issue_ids` is `[]`

And this is not just that one cluster:
- many auto-clusters currently have empty `issue_ids`
- but their member overrides still exist

Why:
- plan schema normalization in [migrations.py](/Users/user_c042661f/Documents/desloppify/desloppify/engine/_plan/schema/migrations.py) is using `_normalize_cluster_issue_id(...)`
- that helper currently only accepts IDs starting with `review::` or `concerns::`
- so when the plan is normalized, it silently drops cluster members for:
  - `subjective::*`
  - `smells::*`
  - `security::*`
  - `dupes::*`
  - and basically every non-review detector

That means:
- `plan_cluster` metadata still points items at `auto/initial-review` via overrides
- but `collapse_clusters()` uses `cluster.issue_ids`
- since `cluster.issue_ids` is empty, there is nothing to collapse
- so `next` shows the dimensions one-by-one instead of one batch cluster card

Concrete evidence from the live plan:
- `auto/initial-review.issue_ids == []`
- but overrides still reference 20 members
- same pattern exists for `auto/test_coverage`, `auto/dupes-exact`, `auto/security`, etc.

So the root cause in one sentence:
- plan schema normalization is incorrectly treating cluster member IDs as if only review/concerns IDs are valid, which wipes auto-cluster membership and prevents `next` from collapsing them into batch cluster items.

I’m going to patch this now in two parts:
1. stop schema normalization from dropping non-review cluster IDs
2. repair current plan clusters from surviving overrides when `issue_ids` is empty

That should make `next` surface the batch cluster the way you expect.

> AGENT

Yes. Root cause is now clear, and it was a real tool bug.

What was wrong:
- `next` only collapses items into a cluster if `plan["clusters"][name]["issue_ids"]` contains the member IDs.
- The live cluster `auto/initial-review` had the right batch action, but `issue_ids` was empty.
- That happened because plan schema normalization in [migrations.py](/Users/user_c042661f/Documents/desloppify/desloppify/engine/_plan/schema/migrations.py) was only treating `review::` and `concerns::` IDs as valid cluster members.
- So it was wiping cluster membership for:
  - `subjective::*`
  - `smells::*`
  - `security::*`
  - `dupes::*`

Make subjective rerun policy explicit and split it into two classes:

1. `unscored`
- always queue

- may defer behind objective backlog
- but must be labeled `deferred`, not hidden ambiguously

3. `under_target`
- do not fully suppress
- keep them visible as queued review work, just lower priority than objective fixes

Why this is the right split:
- `unscored` is mandatory baseline work
- `stale` is freshness work, so deferral is reasonable
- `under_target` is exactly the “score is below target, improve this” case, so hiding it contradicts the product promise

What I would implement:

1. Change queue policy
- in [subjective.py](/Users/user_c042661f/Documents/desloppify/desloppify/engine/_plan/policy/subjective.py)
- `should_inject_to_plan()` for `under_target_ids` should return `True`
- `should_evict_from_plan()` should not evict under-target items just because objective backlog exists

2. Change queue sync
- in [dimensions.py](/Users/user_c042661f/Documents/desloppify/desloppify/engine/_plan/sync/dimensions.py)
- stop pruning under-target subjective IDs when objective backlog exists

One thing: just understand how this works with the 'start of cylce sequence'?

> AGENT

Yes. That is the key constraint, and the plan needs to respect it.

How it works today:

- `start of cycle`
  - unscored subjective dimensions are allowed to surface
  - this is the “initial review” / baseline-establishing phase
- `mid-cycle`
  - once objective work exists, the policy treats subjective reruns as deferrable
  - that is why stale and under-target items get pushed into `subjective_defer_meta`
- `end of cycle`
  - when objective backlog is drained, deferred subjective reruns can surface again
  - that is where stale/under-target review is currently meant to come back

So the current design intent is:
- subjective baseline at cycle start
- objective execution in the middle
- subjective cleanup/rerun at cycle end

The problem is not that this sequence exists.
The problem is that the current implementation lumps two different kinds of subjective work into the same “mid-cycle defer” bucket:

1. `unscored`
- belongs at cycle start
- current behavior is broadly correct

2. `stale`
- reasonable to defer to cycle end
- current behavior is defensible

3. `under_target`
- this is the important one
- these are not “just refresh later” items
- they are active below-target quality deficits
- treating them like stale reruns is what breaks the user contract

So with cycle sequencing in mind, the robust rule becomes:

- `cycle start`
  - show `unscored`
- `mid-cycle`
  - show objective work first
  - keep `under_target` visible, but behind objective work
  - defer `stale`
- `cycle end`
  - surface deferred `stale`
  - keep `under_target` visible as well if anything remains below target

Why this fits the lifecycle better:
- it preserves the start-of-cycle baseline review
- it preserves objective-first execution
- it preserves end-of-cycle stale refresh
- but it stops hiding genuine below-target quality gaps just because the cycle is in progress

So I would revise the rationale slightly:

- the bug is not “subjective work should always ignore cycle sequencing”
- the bug is “under-target subjective work was incorrectly treated as end-of-cycle-only refresh work”

That is the right lifecycle-aware framing.

If you want, I can produce a revised full plan that explicitly centers the start/mid/end-cycle sequence.
